rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. The retention window and resolutions will guide subsequent window trimming, slope, and temperature adjustments.

Halve the gradient slope while holding composition endpoints and temperature fixed to test which crowded pairs respond to slope. The initial elution times suggest this comparison should still finish near or below 10 minutes.

The shallower gradient resolved most of the crowded region but left one nearly coeluting pair. Raising temperature at the same slope tests thermal selectivity and should also create more room below the 10-minute time threshold.

Test a modest temperature reduction to move the remaining close pair away from its apparent selectivity crossover. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature effect while preserving substantial margin below 10 minutes.
Return to the best temperature and make the gradient slightly shallower to spread the remaining close pair. The last peak at 8.56 minutes leaves room for this change without an expected time penalty.

The longer gradient moved the critical pair closer together, so test a steeper gradient instead. This should improve that pair and shorten the run, while checking whether the earlier pair retains sufficient resolution.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shift selectivity and shorten retention, while slightly reducing gradient slope. This tests whether the early pair can reach R ≥ 1.5 without sacrificing resolution of the later close pair.

Use a slope about 3% shallower than injection 7 to improve its two marginal early pairs while preserving the later pair’s resolution margin. The reduced endpoint remains well above the observed elution window, so all peaks should still elute during the gradient.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to bring the marginal early pair above R = 1.5. The later close pair has some resolution margin, and the final peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Injection 9 has reached the maximum CRF; now test a shorter fully resolved separation by raising the starting organic fraction. The narrower gradient also reduces slope, which may compensate for compression of the early peaks.

Keep injection 9 as the maximum-score incumbent and explore a distinctly different temperature-selectivity regime. Holding its gradient fixed will reveal whether lower temperature provides resolution margins that could support a faster gradient.
Raise temperature one step from injection 11 to test whether its lone unresolved pair separates while retention decreases. Injection 9 remains the maximum-score incumbent.

Test an intermediate temperature with a shorter gradient for a potentially faster fully resolved separation. Temperature-dependent order changes suggest another useful selectivity window may exist between 40 and 55 C; injection 9 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Lengthen injection 13’s gradient by one step to test whether its two unresolved early pairs improve at this temperature. The 6.82-minute last peak leaves room to gain resolution without a time penalty.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a substantially higher starting organic fraction for a faster separation in a different selectivity regime. The narrower, shallower gradient may restore separation after an early-pair order reversal, though early-peak compression is a risk.

Test whether lower temperature preserves early retention while a higher starting organic fraction and shorter gradient reduce separation time. This explores a different selectivity regime; injection 9 remains the established maximum-CRF method.

Test a steeper gradient to move injection 16’s nearly coeluting pair farther past its apparent order reversal and shorten the separation. Monitor the late pair at R = 1.55 closely for lost resolution; injection 9 remains the maximum-score incumbent.

Test a 10 C temperature increase at the faster gradient to shift both remaining critical pairs through temperature-dependent selectivity changes. This may yield a shorter fully resolved method, while injection 9 remains the proven maximum-CRF choice.

Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 17’s gradient slope to test composition-dependent selectivity of its unresolved pairs. This also targets a shorter separation; injection 9 remains the maximum-score incumbent.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction, which improved the middle critical pair, with a shallower slope to improve the late pair. This targets full resolution in a shorter separation, while checking for compression of earlier peaks.

Make injection 20’s gradient slightly shallower to improve its sole unresolved pair and add margin to the late pair at R = 1.52. The neighboring pair at R = 2.19 has room to tolerate some selectivity loss, and retention should remain well below 10 minutes.
Injection 21 achieves maximum CRF with the last peak at 4.14 minutes. Raise temperature one step to test whether retention can be shortened further while keeping every pair at R ≥ 1.5.

Return to 25 C and test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to offset the critical pair’s compression. This targets a shorter fully resolved separation, with injection 21 retained as the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Return to the fastest fully resolved starting composition and modestly reduce slope to increase resolution margins. Since maximum CRF is already secured, this tests a more robust alternative that should remain comfortably below the time-penalty threshold.
